Summer is here! As I write this the summer solstice is just a few days away, just shy of a week before
our June meeting. The main event at our June meeting will be a demonstration by Gary Burns on
“Hardening soft and spalted woods with cactus juice so you have wood that can be turned easily
and maintain the figure you want!” This will also be our last meeting of the season before we break
for the summer.
Well, not really the whole summer. Our big summer BBQ bash and GVWG’s 20th Anniversary celebration will be taking place at Dan Breck’s garden estate on the weekend of August 10th. This is not
an event to be missed. Lots more information about this event will be forthcoming.
I was fortunate to be able to spend time at the Richmond Woodcarving Show at the end of May, admiring all of the amazing, lifelike carvings and chatting with the carvers. This year the show was
opening up the field for woodturnings. There weren’t a lot of turnings at the show but those that
were there did garner a lot of interest from the visitors. I think there was a Marco category because
he appeared to have his own section! It was good to see him again and I pestered him to start coming
to meetings again to which he agreed.
I was also especially fortunate to be able to attend and say a few words at the opening of the GVWG’s
The Art of Wood exhibit at the Port Moody Arts Centre where 22 of our members have work on exhibit. I was absolutely blown away by the pieces submitted by our members. Many of them I’d admired before on our Instant Gallery tables but many more were new to me and really opened my eyes
to the amazing talent we have within our club. If you haven’t already done so, do yourself a favour
and please check out the exhibit. It runs until July 11. By the way, Larry was there, too. I think a few
of you may be getting a tap on the shoulder…
Since we have 3 months before our next meeting, the President’s Challenge for September will be,
“What I Learned This Summer”. Challenge yourself to learn a brand-new skill or technique this summer and develop it into a turning for the September meeting.
Have a great summer everyone!

By Steve Hansen
Teach Your Chuck A New Trick
A couple of things arose from my last demo that I’d
like to expound upon. First the jaws. I showed you
a set of sharpened jaws from my 4-jaw scroll chuck.
In my opinion, for holding the harder timbers, the
grip will be improved if the serrations on the jaws
are sharp. In my case that is a Oneway Stronghold
and the jaws are rather blunt as delivered. I believe
sharpening them will allow the chuck to bite deeper
into the fibers of harder timbers and therefore provide a more secure grip. Think cocobolo, the
“ironwoods”, and others that are approaching 2000
pounds-force on the Janka scale. Check it out:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Janka_hardness_test . Should you be inclined to
sharpen a set of your jaws you need a very fine file
that matches the valley of your serrations. In my
case a triangle profile of 120 degrees did the trick.
You also need to file each serration equally and on
all 4 jaws otherwise you run the risk of runout and/
or degrading your grip. My file is from a hobbyist
set of a dozen mini files. I imagine places like
Michaels, Lee Valley, Princess Auto, etc. would carry them.
I also demonstrated using the 4-jaw chuck with only two jaws employed . . .
so that odd-shaped or odd-oriented blanks could be
gripped
and the other two jaws
would otherwise be superfluous or get in the
way. For this application, tower jaws will be
needed. I added an
auxiliary gripper, an
adjustable dog if you
like into the middle of the jaws. Here’s the scoop.
The geometry of the inside of the jaws is cylindrical. Because of this, depending on the shape of the
held blank, it might only be holding on two corners
of each jaw. The dog functions as a third contact
and gripping point to reduce the risk of the blank
deflecting. This works particularly well for triangular shapes. The dog is made from a fine screw that
is fed through a drilled and tapped hole into the

Page 4
GVWG
jaw. It is located roughly middle/centre of the jaw
as shown in the picture below.
Naturally the opposite jaw will have a complimentary dog. This setup will allow you to turn dimensional stock of just about any shape. Warning! Because of the unconventional gripping orientations
that are possible and the reduced holding power of
two less jaws I suggest turning small pieces of less
than 4 inches across. On the creative side, there are
plenty of interesting shapes and figures that can be
derived.
On another note, I power-hone many of my chisels.
I didn’t mention this during the demo, but one
keen-eyed member noticed the nice shine on my
3/8 bowl gouge. I am currently using a seven inch
neoprene wheel impregnated with fine abrasive
which is mounted on a half speed grinder which is
running in reverse – a must for a honing
wheel! I’ve had it a long time and wonder why
they are not more widely available. They do a marvelous job of attaining a very sharp edge. Other
than running the wheel in reverse for safety, the
honing is done using the same methods and implements as for grinding.
Steve
By Bruce Campbell
The Art of Wood - Guild Show at Port
Moody Art Center
Twenty two Guild members collaborated to assemble over a hundred pieces for our second group
exhibition at the Port Moody Arts Center. The
opening of the show on June 6th was well attended
with most of the artists their along with friend and
family and lots of the art-appreciating members of
the community.
A special thanks to Des Wilson and Ed Pretty for
their coordination efforts and Phil and Dan for
their wonderfully innovative display stands.
Janice Cotter – PMAC Gallery Manager and her
staff and volunteers did an outstanding job of setting up the show and I have had LOTS of feedback
for people who have seen the show that are simply
amazed by what they saw.
The show is on until July 11th and I encourage everyone to make the trip to Port Moody to see the
show.

At the May Club Meeting Jay and Lin pulled me
aside and asked me how I would like my bowl
oriented before they took photographed it for
the newsletter. I thoughtlessly said, “It doesn’t
matter.” But the next day I realized that it does
matter. The fact that Jay and Lin had taken
the time to make sure that the photo would present the best image of the piece should have
been met with more consideration by me. Every month Jay, Lin and others spend the meeting recording our best efforts. The work
doesn’t stop there. The photos are then
cropped, catalogued and sent to the Newsletter
for publication where people from all over the
world are able to view our creations.
These reflections got me thinking about all the
others who contribute to making our meetings
and our whole woodturning experience so rewarding. At the risk of forgetting someone,
here is a list of others that come to mind.

Bruce & Larry who facilitate Tech Talk and
Focus on Form and Finish. Bruce not only
facilitates the forum but also writes up each
talk for the newsletter;

the important decisions for the Guild;

I have recently returned from a five day Masterclass in woodturning with Glen Lucas at his
woodturning school in Ireland. Glen, who is renowned for his prolific production turning of salad
bowls, visited us in the Fall where he gave a great
demonstration and follow up class on his techniques. If you get the AAW’s Keep Turning Online
Newsletter you will find in the June 2019 edition
(A Pro’s Guide to a Simple Bowl), a clear description of the techniques he uses to produce a couple
of thousand bowls per year!
Glen’s shop is on his family farm a couple of hours
drive south of Dublin, near the small town of Borris. This particular class had five participants (two
Americans, a Dane a Norwegian and myself), so we
were able to get plenty of individual attention.
With a schedule running from 9am-5pm each day,
including an hour lunch break, we covered the
whole range of topics from wood selection, to tool
sharpening, to lathe maintenance, but spent most
of the time turning a 12 inch platter, a Viking bowl
and some large salad bowls. Each Vicmarc lathe
station has a complete range of well-maintained
chucks, faceplates, and other accessories, so the
turning is very efficient!
Glen is a gifted teacher with infinite patience and a
wonderful sense of humour, so it was a really enjoyable and memorable experience to work with
him over a whole week in beautiful surroundings.
His wife Cornelia, a gourmet cook with a warm and
friendly personality, not only produced outstanding lunches and snacks every day, but arranged a
variety of adventures for accompanying partners
and evening gatherings in local pubs and restaurants.
All in all, it was truly a memorable experience to
work with such a gifted turner who clearly enjoys
teaching others no matter their level of skill. The
surroundings and companionship of the others
added icing to the cake. I would recommend this to
anyone interested in expanding their skill level,
especially as this year Glen will be replacing his
facility with an entirely new and expanded set of
workshops, classrooms and finishing spaces. An
opportunity not to be missed !
by Des WIlson

 Always wear safety goggles or safety glasses that
include side protectors. Use a full face shield for
bowl, vessel, or any turning involving chucks and
faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder
and wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods
of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the tool rest or
tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches,
and knockout bars immediately after use. Never
leave them in place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose clothing, jewelry,
or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating
parts or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the workpiece is
solidly mounted with stout screws (#10 or #12
sheet metal screws as a minimum). Do not use dry
wall or deck screws.
 When turning between centers, be certain the
workpiece is firmly mounted between the headstock driving center and tailstock center.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in place.
 Check that all locking devices on the tailstock and
tool rest assembly (rest and base) are tight before
operating the lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by hand to make
sure it clears the toolrest and bed before turning
the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind and in front
of the workpiece, they are the most likely areas for
a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good
safety habit is to step out of this zone when turning
on the lathe, keeping your hand on the switch in
case you need to turn the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning
it on. Use slower speeds for larger diameters or
rough pieces and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a
piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the
machine to verify why. As a starting point, consult
your operator’s manual for recommended speeds
for a particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed is
compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock with
cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular
shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid
these types of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding
the tool in a controlled but comfortable manner.
Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is
possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless
it is securely tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing, and keep
your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check for damaged
parts, alignment, binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer perYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
Safety Guidelines for Wood Turning

Page 18
GVWG
formance. Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool
for a purpose for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t use a
lathe in damp or wet locations. Do not use in presence of inflammable liquids or gases, and always
keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close
attention to unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop
the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate
machines when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric
cords for damage. Avoid the use of extension
cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn
power off. Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a
complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur while using
saws, especially band and chain saws. Learn and
follow the safety guidelines for this equipment.
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
Safety Guidelines for Wood Turning
